## The senior bar

What separates a senior answer from a mid-level one in this area.

- Accounts for GPU memory and step time with arithmetic (bytes per parameter, activations, bandwidth) and uses it to choose between sharding, accumulation, checkpointing and a bigger machine.
- Knows what each form of parallel training splits and what it communicates, and predicts where scaling stops.
- Designs data pipelines to be idempotent, replayable and correct with respect to time, so that backfills and late data do not corrupt training sets.
- Chooses storage formats and layouts from the read pattern of training, and can explain why small files and random reads are the enemy.
- Treats long runs as failure-prone by default, with checkpointing, preemption handling and resumable data order.
- Makes experiments comparable and reproducible through tracking and lineage, and spends a tuning budget deliberately.

### Data pipelines and ETL (Spark, Beam, Airflow, Flink, Kafka) <span class="demand">39% of postings</span> {#data-pipelines}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="infra.data-pipelines.0"> Choose between batch and streaming from a freshness requirement and say what streaming costs
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="infra.data-pipelines.1"> Explain a Spark job's stages, shuffles and the effect of key skew
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="infra.data-pipelines.2"> Describe how a stream processor gets exactly-once results with checkpoints and idempotent or transactional sinks
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="infra.data-pipelines.3"> Explain event time, watermarks and late data
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="infra.data-pipelines.4"> Design orchestrated tasks that are idempotent and can be backfilled by partition

<details class="qa" id="infra-001">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> When do you build a streaming pipeline instead of a batch one for ML features or training data? What does streaming cost?</summary>

Build streaming only when the value of freshness is demonstrated; batch is the default.

**Batch.** Process bounded data on a schedule (hourly, daily). Simple to reason about,
easy to rerun and backfill, cheap, and complete: each run sees all the data for its
window. Latency is the schedule period plus the run time.

**Streaming.** Process events as they arrive, with results available in seconds. Needed
when a feature loses value quickly: fraud signals from the last minutes, session
context for recommendations, counters that gate abuse.

What streaming costs:

- *Time semantics.* Events arrive late and out of order, so you must define event-time
  windows, watermarks and what happens to late data.
- *State.* Windowed aggregates and joins hold state that must be checkpointed, restored
  and bounded.
- *Operations.* A long-running job with upgrades, rescaling and backpressure, on call
  around the clock.
- *Two code paths.* Training data is usually built in batch from history, while serving
  features come from the stream. If the logic exists twice, the two drift apart.

How to decide:

1. Measure the benefit: evaluate the model with features delayed by an hour or a day. If
   the metric does not move, do not stream.
2. Consider the middle ground: micro-batches every few minutes, or computing the
   freshest features at request time from recent raw events.
3. If you stream, keep one definition of each feature that runs in both modes, or log
   the served feature values and train on those.

Architecturally, the "lambda" pattern runs batch and stream in parallel and merges
them; the "kappa" pattern uses one streaming engine and replays the log for backfills.
One code path is worth a great deal.

**Follow-ups**

- How would you quantify what a fresher feature is worth before building anything?
- What breaks when a backfill is run through a streaming job?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="infra-002">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">debugging</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> A Spark job that builds a training set used to take 40 minutes and now takes 6 hours. How do you find out why?</summary>

Recall how Spark executes: transformations are lazy and build a plan; an action runs it
as stages separated by **shuffles**; each stage is a set of tasks, one per partition.
Slowness is almost always in a shuffle or in a few oversized tasks.

**Look at the UI before the code.**

1. Which stage takes the time? Compare with a previous run.
2. In that stage, compare task durations and shuffle read sizes. A median of seconds
   with a maximum of hours is **skew**; uniformly slow tasks point to volume, resources
   or the plan.
3. Check spill to disk, garbage-collection time, failed and retried tasks.

**Common causes.**

- *Key skew.* One key (a null, a bot account, a default id) holds a large share of the
  rows, so one task does most of a join or aggregation. Fixes: filter or handle the hot
  key separately, salt the key, enable adaptive skew handling.
- *A join that changed strategy.* A table grew past the broadcast threshold, so a cheap
  broadcast join became a shuffle join; or a missing join condition created a partial
  cross product. Read the physical plan.
- *Input growth or layout.* Many more small files, or partition pruning that stopped
  working because of a changed filter or a cast on the partition column, so the job
  scans everything.
- *Too few or too many partitions.* Huge partitions spill and fail; tens of thousands of
  tiny ones drown in overhead.
- *Python UDFs* row by row, where built-in functions or vectorised UDFs would do.
- *Recomputation.* A DataFrame used several times without caching is recomputed from
  the source each time.
- *Cluster.* Fewer executors, preempted nodes, a slow storage backend.

**Then prevent it.** Track input sizes and stage times per run, alert on duration, and
add a data-quality check on the join keys, since skew usually signals a data problem
upstream.

**Follow-ups**

- How does salting a key fix a skewed join, and what does it cost?
- What do you look for in the physical plan?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="infra-003">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> How does a stream processor such as Flink reading from Kafka produce exactly-once results? Explain event time and watermarks while you are at it.</summary>

**Exactly-once.** Messages may be delivered more than once; what can be guaranteed is
that each event affects the result exactly once. Three parts make that true.

1. *Replayable source.* Kafka keeps an ordered log per partition, and a consumer's
   position is an offset. After a failure the job can re-read from a known offset.
2. *Consistent checkpoints.* The engine periodically snapshots the state of all
   operators together with the source offsets that state corresponds to. On failure it
   restores the snapshot and replays from those offsets. Internal state is then as if
   each event had been processed once.
3. *Sinks that do not duplicate.* Replayed events are emitted again, so the sink must be
   either idempotent (an upsert by key, so a repeat overwrites with the same value) or
   transactional (output is committed atomically with the checkpoint, a two-phase
   commit).

Without the third part you have exactly-once state and at-least-once output.

**Event time and watermarks.** Events carry the time they happened, which differs from
when they are processed: mobile clients buffer, partitions lag. Windows defined on
processing time give results that change on replay. Event-time windows are
deterministic, but the engine must decide when a window is complete. A **watermark** is
the engine's assertion that no events older than time $t$ are still expected, typically
the maximum event time seen minus an allowed lateness. When the watermark passes a
window's end, the window fires.

The trade-off: a generous watermark waits longer and loses less; a tight one is fast and
drops or mishandles more late events. Late events can be discarded, sent to a side
output, or used to update an already-emitted result, which downstream consumers must
then tolerate.

For ML, late data means features computed in the stream can differ from what a batch
job would compute later over complete data. That is a source of training-serving skew
unless training uses the logged served values.

**Follow-ups**

- Why is an idempotent sink easier to operate than a transactional one?
- What happens to a windowed feature when a mobile client uploads events a day late?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="infra-004">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> What makes a scheduled data pipeline safe to rerun and to backfill? Describe how you would structure tasks in an orchestrator such as Airflow.</summary>

The property to aim for is **idempotence**: running a task again for the same logical
period produces the same output and no duplicates. With it, retries, reruns after a bug
fix and backfills are routine; without it, each is a risk.

**How to get it.**

- *Parameterise by data interval.* A task processes the interval the scheduler hands it,
  never "now" or "yesterday" computed from the wall clock. Then running it for a date
  last month does the right thing.
- *Write by partition, atomically.* Output goes to a partition keyed by the interval and
  is overwritten as a whole: write to a temporary location, then swap. Never append to
  a shared table from a task that can be retried.
- *Deterministic inputs.* Read input partitions for the same interval, or a pinned
  snapshot, not whatever the source contains at run time.
- *No hidden state.* Everything a task needs comes from its inputs and parameters.

**Structure.**

- A DAG of small tasks with explicit data dependencies, each with one output.
- Sensors or dataset triggers that wait for upstream partitions instead of fixed sleep
  times.
- Validation tasks between stages that fail the run on bad data, so bad partitions are
  not consumed.
- Retries with backoff for transient failures, timeouts, and alerts with an owner.
- Heavy computation in the engine (Spark, the warehouse), with the orchestrator only
  coordinating.

**Backfills.** Rerun a range of intervals after a logic change. Things to plan: the
order and parallelism, downstream tasks that must rerun too, load on shared systems, and
versioning of the output so that models trained on the old data can still be traced.
Late-arriving data needs the same mechanism: reprocess the last few days routinely.

A useful test: can you delete any output partition and regenerate it with one command?

**Follow-ups**

- A task appends rows and was retried after a timeout. What is in the table now?
- How do you backfill a year of data without overloading the source system?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="infra-005">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">coding</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> In PySpark, keep only the latest record per user from an event table, then compute daily distinct users and revenue per country. What should the interviewer hear about performance and correctness?</summary>

```python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window

# 1. Latest record per user, with a deterministic tie-break.
w = Window.partitionBy("user_id").orderBy(
    F.col("updated_at").desc(), F.col("ingest_id").desc())
latest = (events
          .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w))
          .filter(F.col("rn") == 1)
          .drop("rn"))

# 2. Daily aggregates.
daily = (events
         .withColumn("day", F.to_date("event_ts"))
         .groupBy("day", "country")
         .agg(F.countDistinct("user_id").alias("users"),
              F.sum("amount").alias("revenue")))

(daily.write.mode("overwrite")
      .partitionBy("day")
      .parquet("s3://bucket/daily_country/"))
```

Correctness points:

- `dropDuplicates(["user_id"])` keeps an arbitrary row per key; use a window with an
  explicit order when "latest" matters, and add a tie-breaker so reruns give the same
  answer.
- Decide what happens to null keys and null amounts; `sum` ignores nulls, and all null
  user ids land in one group.
- Time zones: `to_date` uses the session time zone. State which day boundary the
  business means.
- Duplicated events inflate revenue. Deduplicate on an event id before aggregating.

Performance points:

- Both steps shuffle by key. A hot key, such as a null or a bot user, creates one huge
  task.
- Exact distinct counts are expensive; `approx_count_distinct` is much cheaper when a
  small error is acceptable.
- Filter to the needed date range first so that partition pruning applies, and select
  only the columns used.
- Overwriting only the partitions being written needs dynamic partition overwrite mode;
  the default static mode replaces the whole table. This is what makes the job safe to
  rerun for one day.

**Follow-ups**

- Write the first step in SQL.
- How would you make the daily job incremental instead of recomputing all history?

</details>


### GPU computing and accelerators <span class="demand">28% of postings</span> {#gpu}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="infra.gpu.0"> Estimate training memory from parameters, gradients, optimizer state and activations
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="infra.gpu.1"> Distinguish allocated from reserved memory and diagnose an out-of-memory error that appears late in a run
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="infra.gpu.2"> Say which hardware properties matter for a given training or inference workload

<details class="qa" id="infra-006">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">derivation</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Estimate the GPU memory needed to train a model with one billion parameters. What are the components and which one usually dominates?</summary>

Four components.

**1. Parameters.** $10^9$ parameters at 4 bytes in 32-bit floats: 4 GB.

**2. Gradients.** One per parameter, same size: 4 GB.

**3. Optimizer state.** Adam and AdamW keep two moment estimates per parameter: 8 GB.
SGD with momentum keeps one: 4 GB.

So the static cost with AdamW is 16 bytes per parameter, 16 GB here, before any data has
passed through the model. Mixed precision does not reduce this part: under automatic
mixed precision the stored weights and the optimizer state stay in 32-bit floats.

**4. Activations.** Every intermediate tensor needed by the backward pass is kept until
it has been used. This scales with batch size, sequence length or resolution, width and
depth. For a transformer, each layer keeps several tensors of shape
$[B, T, d]$ and, unless a fused attention kernel is used, attention maps of shape
$[B, h, T, T]$. For large batches or long sequences this component dominates, and it is
the part mixed precision halves.

Also allow for the framework's allocator cache and fragmentation, library workspaces,
and a temporary peak during the optimizer step.

**Levers by component.**

- Activations: smaller batch with gradient accumulation; mixed precision; activation
  (gradient) checkpointing, which recomputes activations in the backward pass at the
  price of roughly one extra forward pass; shorter sequences; memory-efficient
  attention.
- Optimizer state and gradients: sharding across GPUs (ZeRO or FSDP); an 8-bit or
  factored optimizer; training fewer parameters (adapters).
- Parameters: sharding; lower-precision frozen weights when fine-tuning adapters.

Inference needs only the parameters and one layer's activations at a time, which is why
a model that trains on 40 GB can serve on a fraction of that.

**Follow-ups**

- Why does automatic mixed precision not halve the parameter and optimizer memory?
- Doubling the sequence length quadruples memory in one case and doubles it in another. Which is which?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="infra-007">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">debugging</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> A training job dies with a CUDA out-of-memory error several hours in, although the first thousands of steps ran fine. How do you debug it?</summary>

An error that appears late is rarely "the model is too big". Something grows, or a rare
input is large.

**1. Read the message and the counters.** It reports allocated and reserved memory.
*Allocated* is memory held by live tensors; *reserved* is what the framework's caching
allocator has taken from the device. Log both, and the peak, every N steps.

- Allocated memory climbing steadily means a **leak of references**.
- Flat allocated memory with a sudden failure means a **large batch**.
- Reserved far above allocated means **fragmentation**.

**2. Leaks of references.**

- Accumulating a tensor that still carries its graph, such as `total_loss += loss`
  instead of `loss.item()`. The whole graph of every step stays alive.
- Appending outputs or activations to a Python list for logging.
- Evaluation without `torch.no_grad()`, so graphs are built for nothing.
- A caught exception whose traceback keeps tensors alive.

**3. Input-dependent peaks.** With variable-length sequences or image sizes, memory is
set by the largest batch, which may first appear hours in. Log the batch shape at
failure. Fix with a token budget per batch instead of a fixed batch size, bucketing by
length, a hard cap on length, and a test at startup that runs the worst-case batch.

**4. Fragmentation.** Many allocations of varying size leave free memory in pieces too
small to use. Mitigate by making shapes more regular (bucketing, padding to a few
sizes) and by the allocator's configuration options; consult the current PyTorch
memory-management notes for the exact settings.

**5. Other processes.** A second job or a zombie process on the same device, or an
evaluation run that starts while training memory is still held.

**6. Periodic events.** Evaluation, checkpointing or logging hooks every N steps that
allocate extra memory.

Calling the cache-emptying function in a loop rarely fixes anything: it returns cached
blocks to the device but does not free live tensors.

**Follow-ups**

- What is the difference between allocated and reserved memory?
- How would you catch the worst-case batch before the run starts?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="infra-008">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> You have a fixed budget for training hardware. Which properties of a GPU and of the machine around it matter, and how do you choose between fewer large GPUs and more small ones?</summary>

Match the hardware to what limits the workload.

**Properties of the GPU.**

- *Memory capacity.* A hard constraint: it sets the largest model, batch and sequence
  length without sharding or accumulation, and is the first thing to check.
- *Compute throughput* at the precision you train in, including support for the
  half-precision formats you plan to use.
- *Memory bandwidth*, which bounds many operations more than raw arithmetic does.
- *Links between GPUs* inside a node, which determine how well multi-GPU training
  scales.

**Properties of the machine.**

- CPU cores and RAM per GPU for data loading and preprocessing. Starving the GPU with too
  few cores is a common waste.
- Local NVMe for dataset caches and checkpoints.
- Network interconnect between nodes, if a job spans nodes.
- Power and cooling, for on-premises hardware.

**Fewer large or more small?**

- If one model does not fit in a small GPU's memory, large GPUs avoid the engineering and
  communication cost of sharding. Memory is the deciding factor more often than speed.
- If the workload is many independent jobs (hyperparameter sweeps, evaluation, small
  fine-tunes), more small GPUs give more parallel experiments per unit of money and
  less waste from one job occupying a large device.
- For one large job, scaling across many GPUs is sublinear, so eight devices do not give
  eight times the throughput; within a single node it is usually close, across nodes it
  depends on the interconnect.
- Availability and price per useful hour (including queue time and preemption) often
  matter more than list performance.

**Method.** Benchmark your own training step on the candidates and compute cost per
unit of work, such as dollars per million training tokens or per epoch, not price per
hour. Include utilisation: an expensive GPU that sits idle half the day costs twice its
rate.

**Follow-ups**

- Which workload would you put on older, cheaper GPUs?
- How do you compare hardware when the available benchmarks are for a different model?

</details>


### Cluster scheduling and compute orchestration (Kubernetes, Slurm, Ray) <span class="demand">26% of postings</span> {#cluster}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="infra.cluster.0"> Compare Kubernetes, Slurm and Ray for training workloads
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="infra.cluster.1"> Explain quotas, priorities, preemption, gang scheduling and fragmentation on a shared GPU cluster
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="infra.cluster.2"> Design checkpoint and restart so a preempted job loses minutes, not hours

<details class="qa" id="infra-009">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">trade-off</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">AI</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Compare Kubernetes, Slurm and Ray for running ML training. When would you choose each?</summary>

They sit at different layers and are often combined.

**Slurm.** A batch scheduler from high-performance computing. You submit a job
requesting nodes, GPUs and time; it queues, then runs on bare metal. Strengths:
designed for multi-node tightly coupled jobs, with gang scheduling, fair-share
priorities, partitions, preemption and job arrays; low overhead; researchers know it.
Weaknesses: little support for long-running services, containers are an add-on, and
weaker isolation and ecosystem integration.

**Kubernetes.** A container orchestrator built for services. Strengths: one platform for
training, serving and data jobs; containers and isolation by default; autoscaling of
nodes; a large ecosystem. Weaknesses: the default scheduler places pods one at a time
and knows nothing of queues, quotas across teams or all-or-nothing placement for a
multi-worker job, so training needs a batch scheduling layer and job operators on top
(such as Kueue, Volcano, Kubeflow's training operators). More layers to operate.

**Ray.** A distributed computing framework for Python, not a cluster manager. It
provides tasks, actors and a shared object store, with libraries for data processing,
training, tuning and serving. Strengths: one programming model from a laptop to a
cluster, good for heterogeneous pipelines, hyperparameter search and RL workloads with
many actors. It runs on top of Kubernetes, Slurm or virtual machines, which still do
the resource allocation.

Choosing:

- A research cluster with large multi-node training jobs and users who want to submit
  scripts: Slurm.
- A company that already runs services on Kubernetes and wants one platform, elastic
  cloud capacity and tight integration with serving: Kubernetes plus a batch layer.
- Python-centric workloads that mix data processing, training and tuning in one
  application: Ray on whichever of the two you have.

What matters more than the choice: queues and quotas per team, preemption with
checkpointing, visibility into why a job is waiting, and accounting of GPU hours.

**Follow-ups**

- What is gang scheduling and why does a default Kubernetes scheduler get it wrong?
- How do Ray actors differ from tasks, and where would you use each?

</details>

<details class="qa" id="infra-010">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span><span class="tag tag-rep" title="A third-party site lists a question on this topic as asked in an interview">asked at Anthropic</span> On a shared GPU cluster, how do quotas, priorities and preemption work, and why can GPUs sit idle while jobs are waiting?</summary>

**The policy tools.**

- *Quota.* Each team has a guaranteed share of GPUs. Guarantees prevent starvation.
- *Borrowing.* Idle quota is lent to other teams so that capacity is not wasted. Borrowed
  capacity is reclaimable.
- *Priority.* Classes such as production, interactive, standard and best-effort order the
  queue and decide who may preempt whom.
- *Preemption.* When a team wants its guaranteed GPUs back, or a higher-priority job
  arrives, borrowed or lower-priority jobs are stopped. This is acceptable only if jobs
  checkpoint and resume automatically.
- *Fair share.* Priority decays with recent usage, so a heavy user does not hold the
  queue indefinitely.

**Why GPUs idle while jobs wait.**

- *Fragmentation.* Free GPUs are scattered: 16 free in total, but no node has 8, so an
  8-GPU job cannot start. Bin-packing placement (fill nodes before opening new ones) and
  occasional defragmentation by migrating small jobs reduce this.
- *Gang scheduling.* A distributed job needs all its workers at once. A scheduler that
  starts workers one by one lets two large jobs each hold half of what they need and
  deadlock. All-or-nothing admission prevents it.
- *Head-of-line blocking.* A large job at the front waits for resources while small jobs
  behind it could run. Backfilling runs small jobs in the gaps if they will finish
  before the large job's reservation starts, which requires time limits on jobs.
- *Constraints.* Jobs pinned to a GPU type, zone or node pool.
- *Reserved but unused.* Interactive sessions and notebooks holding GPUs at zero
  utilisation. Idle detection and time limits recover them.
- *Other resources.* Not enough CPU or memory on the node next to the free GPU.

**Measure** allocation rate and utilisation separately. Allocated-but-idle GPUs are a
user-behaviour problem; unallocated GPUs with a queue are a scheduler problem. Show
users why their job is pending.

**Follow-ups**

- How does backfilling work, and why does it need job time limits?
- A team complains its jobs are preempted too often. What do you look at?

<div class="reported">

**Reported in interviews** (candidate reports on third-party sites, not verified)

- Anthropic, Software Engineer, Aug 2026: Schedule one-GPU and eight-GPU jobs fairly ([PracHub](https://prachub.com/interview-questions/schedule-one-gpu-and-eight-gpu-model-jobs))

</div>

</details>

<details class="qa" id="infra-011">
<summary><span class="tag tag-senior">senior</span><span class="tag tag-type">design</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span> Design checkpointing and restart for long training jobs on preemptible capacity, so that a preemption costs minutes and needs no human.</summary>

**What a checkpoint must contain to resume exactly.**

- Model parameters.
- Optimizer state (moments), learning-rate scheduler state and the global step.
- Gradient scaler state under mixed precision; EMA weights if used.
- Random number generator states.
- Data position: epoch, shard and offset, or the sampler's state, so that the resumed
  run neither repeats nor skips data.
- The configuration and code version, to refuse resuming with a mismatched setup.

Forgetting the optimizer or scheduler state is the classic bug: the loss jumps after
resume and the learning rate restarts its warm-up.

**Writing it safely.**

- Write to a temporary name, then rename atomically, so a preemption during a write
  never leaves a corrupt latest checkpoint. Keep the last few and verify on load.
- Write to local disk first and upload asynchronously if the remote store is slow, so
  the training loop does not stall.
- For sharded training, each rank writes its shard in parallel.
- Choose the interval from the cost of a checkpoint and the preemption rate: frequent
  enough that expected lost work is small, rare enough that writing is a few percent of
  run time. Time-based intervals are more robust than step-based ones.

**Reacting to preemption.**

- Handle the termination signal: the platform usually gives a notice of tens of seconds
  to a couple of minutes. Finish the current step, write a checkpoint, exit with a code
  that means "retry".
- If the notice is too short for a full checkpoint, rely on the periodic one.

**Restarting without a human.**

- The job is submitted with a retry policy; on start it looks for the latest valid
  checkpoint under its run id and resumes, otherwise it starts fresh. The same code
  path handles first start and restart.
- Metrics and logs continue under the same run id, with resumes marked.
- Evaluation and export jobs watch for new checkpoints instead of living in the
  training process.

**Test it.** Kill the job at random points in CI and compare the resumed loss curve
with an uninterrupted run.

**Follow-ups**

- The loss spikes after every resume. What did the checkpoint miss?
- How do you make the data order resumable with a shuffled, sharded dataset?

</details>


### Distributed / large-scale training <span class="demand">16% of postings</span> {#dist-training}

- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="infra.dist-training.0"> Say what data parallelism, tensor and pipeline parallelism and parameter sharding each split and communicate
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="infra.dist-training.1"> Write a DDP training loop and list what changes relative to one GPU
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="infra.dist-training.2"> Compare synchronous all-reduce training with asynchronous parameter-server training
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="infra.dist-training.3"> Pick techniques to fit a model that exceeds one GPU's memory
- <input type="checkbox" class="chk" data-chk="infra.dist-training.4"> Derive a checkpoint interval from checkpoint cost and failure rate

<details class="qa" id="infra-012">
<summary><span class="tag tag-core">core</span><span class="tag tag-type">concept</span><span class="tag tag-track">MLE</span> <span class="tag tag-track">RE</span><span class="tag tag-rep" title="A third-party site lists a question on this topic as asked in an interview">asked at Google, Nvidia</span> What are the ways to parallelise training across GPUs? Say what each one splits and what it has to communicate.</summary>

| Method | Splits | Communicates | Use when |
|-|-|-|-|
| Data parallelism (DDP) | The batch. Every GPU holds a full model replica and processes a different slice | Gradients, once per step (all-reduce) | The model fits on one GPU and you want throughput |
| Sharded data parallelism (ZeRO, FSDP) | Also the parameters, gradients and optimizer state, each GPU owning a shard | Parameters gathered layer by layer for the forward and backward pass; gradients reduced back to their owners | The model plus optimizer state does not fit on one GPU |
| Tensor parallelism | Individual weight matrices within a layer, across GPUs | Activations inside every layer | Layers too large for one GPU; needs very fast links, so usually within a node |
| Pipeline parallelism | The layers, as consecutive stages on different GPUs | Activations at stage boundaries, and their gradients | Very deep models; uses micro-batches to keep all stages busy |

Details worth knowing:

- **Data parallelism** averages gradients, so the effective batch is the per-GPU batch
  times the number of GPUs. The learning rate and warm-up usually need retuning for the
  larger batch.
- **ZeRO** comes in stages: shard the optimizer state, then also the gradients, then
  also the parameters. Each stage saves more memory and adds communication. FSDP
  corresponds to the last stage: a layer's full parameters exist on a GPU only while
  that layer is computing.
- **Pipeline parallelism** leaves stages idle at the start and end of each batch (the
  "bubble"); more micro-batches shrink it.
- **Tensor parallelism** communicates inside every layer, so its cost is dominated by
  link speed.

Large runs combine them: tensor parallelism inside a node, pipeline across a few nodes,
data parallelism across the rest.

Scaling stops when communication or the input pipeline, not computation, sets the step
time, or when the larger effective batch stops improving optimisation per sample.

**Follow-ups**

- Why does FSDP save memory compared with DDP, and what does it pay?
- Which of these would you combine for a model ten times too large for one GPU?
